title: DriveWorld-VLA: unified world modeling + planning in latent space
one_liner: A self-driving car model that learns to imagine the future in a compressed space and uses those imagined scenes to plan better actions.
lead: When a self-driving car decides what to do, it needs two skills: predicting what the world will look like next (world modeling) and choosing the best action now. Most systems keep these two tasks separate, so predictions do not help planning. DriveWorld-VLA merges them by having the planner read predictions directly from the predictor's brain, so imagining the future changes the plan.

problem.h2: Why separate prediction and planning breaks autonomous driving
paras: A self-driving car has two jobs at every moment: predict what the road and other cars will do next, and decide which steering and throttle command is safest. Today, most cars do these two jobs in separate brains. The prediction brain imagines the future scene. The planning brain picks an action. But the two brains do not talk to each other deeply—the planner does not read the prediction brain's internal thoughts about why the future will unfold a certain way.

A beginner might try to run prediction and planning side-by-side: predict future frames, then search over possible actions to find the one that leads to the best imagined outcome. But this is slow and clunky because the prediction brain runs in pixel space (millions of numbers), so imagining ten seconds ahead fills memory—storing raw image data is expensive. The planner then has to decode pixels to extract what matters, which is inefficient and error-prone: the planner guesses which parts of the prediction matter for steering, wasting effort on road texture when it should focus on the position of that oncoming truck.

callout.html: The planner and predictor use different mental representations, so predicting the future does not directly change how the plan is made.

panels.title: 1. Two separate brains
panels.caption: Today, prediction and planning are separate systems with weak links.

panels.title: 2. Predictor imagines pixels
panels.caption: Predictor generates full future images—millions of pixels, most irrelevant.

panels.title: 3. Planner ignores prediction brain
panels.viz_args: Planner reads pixels, not predictor's reasons
panels.caption: Planner decodes images but misses the predictor's learned patterns.

panels.title: 4. Both read compressed space
panels.caption: New: predictor and planner both think in the same compact space.

panels.title: 5. Planner steers based on predictor's thoughts
panels.caption: Planner reads prediction brain's internal representation to decide steering.

steps.text: Predictor learns a compact mental representation of the scene from images.
Predictor rolls forward this compressed representation to imagine next moments.
Planner takes predictor's internal compressed thoughts (lists of numbers), not decoded images.
Planner asks: if I steer left, how does that change the predictor's mental picture?
Planner chooses the action that leads to the safest imagined scene, because steering that leads to close oncoming traffic gets lower scores than steering that keeps distance.

object.h2: The one thing the paper changes
paras: The paper changes the bridge between prediction and planning. Instead of the planner reading pixel images from the predictor, the planner reads the predictor's internal compressed thought-lists (lists of numbers encoding what the predictor learned about the scene) directly.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: scene representation alignment
hidden.name: representation alignment score
paras: The paper's core insight is measuring whether the predictor's internal compressed thoughts (lists of numbers) actually encode the information the planner needs. A thought-list is well-aligned if it captures road position, vehicle locations, and motion—all in one compact set of numbers. A poorly-aligned thought-list wastes space on irrelevant details like pavement texture.

The paper uses shared training: both the predictor and planner tune the same compressed representation simultaneously. As they train, the representation becomes aligned because both systems learn to emphasize the features that help their own task. The planner learns to value road edges and traffic; the predictor learns to keep track of them too.

heat.caption: Darker means the hidden representation cares more about that feature. Boxes with borders are the most critical for safe driving.

reads.html: The paper measures alignment by checking if both the predictor and planner improve together when they share the same compressed thought-space.

The shared compressed thought-space enables tightly-integrated vision-language-action and world models at the representation level, where the planner can assess action impact on future scene evolution in the same compressed dimensions the predictor uses, because both systems are forced to emphasize the same features—if the predictor encodes truck position, the planner learns to read truck position, so they speak the same language.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: shared compression gains alignment
paras: The planner needs to answer questions like: if I steer left, will I hit the oncoming car? To answer this, it must simulate future scenes. But simulating full pixel-images is expensive and wastes computation on irrelevant details. The insight is that the predictor already solves a related problem: given the current image, predict the next image.

If the predictor and planner both work in the same compressed thought-space, they develop a shared language. When the predictor learns to encode road position in one thought-list, the planner learns to read that same thought-list to check if steering left would collide. They are forced to agree on what matters, because they share the same internal representation.

The mechanism: training the planner and predictor together means their errors push back against each other. If the predictor wastes space on irrelevant details, the planner learns not to trust those details and ignores them. If the planner needs road position to make good steering choices, the predictor learns to emphasize road position in its thought-space because doing so helps the planner succeed. Over time, the thought-space organizes itself around what is actually useful for safe driving.

Predictor rolls thought-lists forward in time
Planner evaluates steering actions against predictions

math.words: Total loss is the prediction error plus the planning error, both measured in the shared thought-space. The prediction error asks: did the next real world-state match my imagined next thought-vector? The planning error asks: did my chosen action lead to a safe outcome in the imagined future?
symbols: combined loss (error) for both prediction and planning
prediction loss: how wrong the predicted thought-vector was
the actual compressed thought-vector of the next moment
planning loss: safety and comfort of the chosen action
the steering and throttle command the planner picked
the imagined thought-vectors over the next few seconds

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Imagine predicting one moment ahead. Real next thought-vector is [0.8, 0.3, 0.6] (road ahead, left lane free, slow oncoming traffic).

Planner chose steering angle 5 degrees. Simulation in that predicted thought-space says: road stays clear (good), left lane opens up (good). Planning loss = 0.1 (small penalty because outcome is safe).
Total loss = 0.0075 + 0.1 = 0.1075. Both systems learn from this: predictor improves prediction, planner learns that this steering angle is safe.

math.note: Sharing the thought-space means both systems optimize for the same compressed representation, so they naturally align on what matters for safe autonomous driving.

charts.title: Separate prediction and planning
charts.note: Planner cannot use predictor's internal thoughts because the two systems do not share representations, so even accurate predictions sit in pixels that the planner must decode—this decoding step loses information and adds latency, preventing predictions from improving driving safety.

charts.title: Unified latent-space model
charts.note: Planner reads predictor's thoughts directly in the shared thought-space, so better predictions immediately make driving safer because the planner is reading the exact representation the predictor improved—no decoding step, no information loss.

items.html: If the encoder squeezes the world too tightly, both predictor and planner lose important detail (like the exact position of a cyclist). The car might miss small obstacles.
If training data is mostly highway driving, the predictor learns to encode highway features very precisely but fails to generalize to crowded city intersections where pedestrians move unpredictably.

items.b: Planner cannot distinguish prediction from reality.
items.html: The planner must remember that it is reading imagined thought-lists, not actual sensor readings. If it treats all thought-lists equally, it might steer aggressively based on a hallucinated obstacle.
The encoder size and training data balance are tuned so the thought-space captures essential driving features without overfitting to noise or hallucinating absent threats.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple autonomous-driving simulator with a 2D bird's-eye-view. The car sees obstacles, lane markings, and traffic. Train a separate-system baseline: one neural network for predicting future obstacles, another for planning steering. Train the unified model: shared encoder, predictor, and planner all using the same compressed thought-space. On unseen road layouts, measure which system avoids collisions more reliably and whether the unified system's predictions correlate with the planner's steering choices.
demo.closing: The unified model must show that better predictions lead directly to safer steering, because the planner reads the prediction brain's internal thoughts.
